title: Pointers in Depth: Arithmetic, const, Arrays & References

chapters.title: Walk an array with a pointer

scenes.say: Add one to a pointer and it moves four bytes, or eight. By the end, you'll read const int star const aloud, and know why sizeof lies in a function.
Today you will do three things. Walk an array using pointer arithmetic. Tell pointers, references and arrays apart, with their const rules. And spot the pointer bugs that crash programs.
lines: Walk an array with pointer arithmetic
Spot the bugs that crash programs

scenes.title: Where does p + 2 land?
scenes.statement: An int pointer points at the first of four ints. Where does p plus two point, and what is q minus p?
scenes.say: Four ints in a row, and a pointer p on the first. Add two. Where does it land? Eight bytes along, not two.

scenes.head: p + 2 means two ints, not two bytes
scenes.say: An int array at hex one thousand. Four bytes each. P points at the first. Now q is p plus two. Q lands on the third, thirty. Subtract: q minus p is two elements, not eight bytes.

scenes.head: The step size comes from the type
scenes.say: An int pointer steps four bytes. A double pointer, eight. A void pointer has no step size, so no arithmetic. And a of two is star of a plus two: subscripting is pointer arithmetic.
Your turn. Start the pointer at the second element, then step two. Which value do you read? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Walking off the end
scenes.say: Forty. P starts at the second element. Two steps on is the fourth, forty. Now the edge. One past the last is legal to hold and compare, but never to read. Anything further is undefined. So is subtracting pointers from different objects.

scenes.title: Pointer, reference, or both?
scenes.statement: Three declarations bind to an int. Which one can be null, which one is just another name, and which one grabs a temporary?

example.input: int* p, int& r, int&& rr
example.output: p holds an address; r aliases; rr grabs

scenes.say: Star, ampersand, double ampersand. Three symbols on the same int, and interviewers love asking which does what.

scenes.head: What each one binds to
scenes.say: Here is x, holding five. P is its own variable, holding x's address. It can be null, and re-pointed. R is not a new variable, just another name for x. That is an l value reference. An l value is anything with a name, so you can take its address. A temporary is an unnamed value. And rr binds to the temporary ten, keeping it alive as long as rr lives.

scenes.head: Why double ampersand exists
scenes.say: Why does the r value reference exist? Overloading. F of x picks the l value version. F of forty two picks the r value one. S t d colon colon move casts x to an r value. Moves rely on this to steal.
Your turn. We declare rr as an r value reference to five. Then we call f of rr. Which overload runs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: After `int&& rr = 5;`, which overload does `f(rr)` call?

scenes.head: A name is always an l value
scenes.say: The l value one. Rr has type r value reference, but it has a name, so the expression rr is an l value. You can take its address. To pass it on as a temporary, cast it again with move.

notes.text: a name is an l value

scenes.head: Pointer, l value ref, r value ref
scenes.say: A pointer is an object holding an address. Null? Only the pointer. Re-pointing? Only the pointer. Typical use? Optional access, passing without copying, and moves.

scenes.head: A reference, a pointer: same machine code
scenes.say: Two functions. One takes a reference, one a constant pointer. Compile both, and the machine code is identical. A stored reference is a hidden pointer, dereferenced for you.

scenes.head: You can only observe the object
scenes.say: The output is 7 4 1 8. Everything you observe goes to the referred object. Size of r is the size of an int. Address of r is x's address. A struct holding a reference is usually pointer sized, here eight, but the standard does not promise it.

scenes.title: Hold any address, or change a pointer
scenes.statement: Two puzzles. Store the address of any object in one pointer type. And let a function change the caller's pointer.

example.output: v holds any address; p gets a new target

scenes.say: Two puzzles. One pointer that can hold the address of anything. And a function that points the caller's own pointer somewhere new.

scenes.head: A void pointer: an address, type erased
scenes.say: X holds forty two. Any object pointer converts to void star automatically. V now holds x's address. But it forgets the type. So you can't dereference it, and you can't add to it. To use the data, cast back with static cast to the real type.

scenes.head: Two classic interview points
scenes.say: First, in C plus plus a void pointer needs an explicit cast to become an int pointer. C allows it silently. That is why malloc's result needs a cast. Second, the compiler trusts you. Cast to double and it compiles. Size the block for that type, or the write runs past its end.

scenes.head: A pointer to a pointer: follow the arrows
scenes.say: Now two stars. X is forty two. P is an int star holding x's address. Pp is an int star star holding p's address. Each star follows one arrow. Star pp is p. Star star pp is forty two. So assigning ninety nine through it changes x itself.

items.label: int** pp
items.cue: Pp is an int star star

scenes.say: Your turn. This function takes a plain int pointer and assigns it a new heap int. We call it with our null pointer. Afterwards, what is our pointer? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `void make(int* p) { p = new int(7); }` After `make(q)`, `q` is...

scenes.head: Pointer to pointer, or reference to pointer
scenes.say: Still null. The function changed its own copy, and leaked the int. Pass the address of q, and it writes into q itself. In C plus plus, a reference to a pointer does the same, more cleanly.

scenes.title: Which const locks what?
scenes.statement: Three declarations differ only in where const sits. Read each aloud, and say what you may change.

example.input: const int* p; int* const p;

scenes.say: Where does const go? Left of the star, or right? Same words, different locks. Say each aloud, and say what it locks.

scenes.head: Three declarations, three locks
scenes.say: Read right to left. P1 is a pointer to a const int: re-point it, but never write through it. P2 is a const pointer to an int: write through it, but never re-point. P3 locks both. And a const pointer must be initialized.
Your turn. Here is p2, an int star const. Which statement compiles? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: For `int* const p = &a;` which line compiles?

scenes.head: Two things to lock
scenes.say: Only the second. P2 locks the pointer, not the int. Each declaration has two things to lock: the pointer, and the int. Const left of the star locks the int. Const right of it locks the pointer. So p1 locks the value. P2, the pointer. P3, both.

scenes.head: The trap: pointer to const isn't const
scenes.say: The classic trap. A pointer to const only blocks writes through that pointer. The int itself isn't const. A can still change, and star p sees ten. That's why parameters use const int star: a promise to only read.

scenes.title: Return the address of a local?
scenes.statement: A function builds a local int and returns its address. It compiles. Is the pointer safe to use afterwards?
scenes.say: Your function builds a local, returns its address, and compiles cleanly. Candidates answer that it works, because they tried it once. Does it?

scenes.head: The frame is gone, the address isn't
scenes.say: Bad gets a stack frame, and x lives in it. It returns x's address, and p holds it. Then bad returns, and the frame is gone. P still points there. Next, other reuses those bytes. Star p might print seven.

scenes.head: Compilers catch the simple case
scenes.say: Compilers warn on the simple case, for pointers, and for references, which are addresses underneath, so they dangle too. Pass the address through another variable, and the warning can vanish. Treat warnings as errors, and run Address Sanitizer.

panels.label: two bugs

output.text:
warning: address of local variable ‘x’ returned
warning: reference to local variable ‘x’ returned

scenes.head: Four functions, four returns
scenes.say: Four small functions. Local address first. Then a reference to a local. Then a literal. Last, a parameter's address.
Your turn. Four functions each return something. Which result is still valid after the function ends? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Which returned value is still valid after the function ends?

scenes.head: What to return instead
scenes.say: A string literal. Literals live in static storage, so that is safe. Otherwise, return by value, which is cheap. A static local lives forever, but it is shared state. Or return a unique pointer, so the caller owns it.

scenes.title: Dereference a null pointer?
scenes.statement: A pointer is nullptr. What does star p do, and can a try block catch the damage?
scenes.say: Now the other half. A null pointer, then a star on it. Candidates say it throws, so a try block catches it. Does it?

scenes.head: From star p to segmentation fault
scenes.say: Null is address zero, and the page at zero is never mapped. So star p makes the processor fault. The operating system sends S I G S E G V: segmentation fault. On Windows, an access violation.

items.label: OS
items.cue: S I G S E G V

scenes.head: Not an exception, and not always a crash
scenes.say: No. It is a signal, not an exception. And it is undefined behavior, so a crash is not even guaranteed. Since p was dereferenced, the optimizer may assume p is not null, and delete the check. Linux had this very bug.

steps.cue: may assume p is not null

scenes.head: Four ways to avoid it
scenes.say: Check pointers that may legitimately be null, before using them. If a value must exist, take a reference. For maybe a value, optional is clearer than null. And in testing, the undefined behavior sanitizer reports a null dereference with file and line.

scenes.title: Array or pointer?
scenes.statement: An array name looks like a pointer. Are they the same? What does sizeof say about each, inside and outside a function?
scenes.say: Four ints, and a pointer to them. Same thing? Ask size of about each. Most candidates get the function case wrong.

scenes.head: Storage versus an address
scenes.say: An array is the elements themselves: four ints, side by side, sixteen bytes. No address is stored anywhere. A pointer is a separate variable holding an address, eight bytes. Write p equals arr, and the array decays to a pointer to its first element. Size of arr is sixteen. Size of p is eight.
Your turn. A function takes a parameter written as int a of four, and prints size of a. What does it print on a sixty four bit machine? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Where decay bites: parameters
scenes.say: Eight. The array decays at the call, and the four in brackets is ignored. The parameter is really an int pointer. So inside print, size of is the pointer size. In main, sixteen. That's why C style functions pass the length separately.

scenes.head: When it doesn't decay, and the fix
scenes.say: Decay isn't everywhere. Size of and ampersand see the real array, and a reference keeps the full type. So a template can take the array by reference and deduce N as four. Modern code uses array, which never decays, or span.

panels.code:
auto  q = &arr;       // int(*)[4]
auto& r = arr;        // int(&)[4]

template <size_t N>
void show(int (&a)[N]);   // N is 4

void show(span<int> s);   // C++20
array<int, 4> safe{};     // never decays

scenes.head: Array versus pointer
scenes.say: An array is storage. A pointer is an address. Size of an array gives all its bytes, a pointer just eight. Arrays cannot be assigned. The address of an array is a pointer to the whole array. And an array knows its size, a pointer does not.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is pointer arithmetic? Adding n moves n elements, not n bytes. Example? Plus two on an int pointer is eight bytes. Valid where? Inside one array, or one past its end.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Pointer versus reference? A pointer holds an address. A reference is an alias. And double ampersand? An alias of a temporary. How is a reference stored? Usually a hidden const pointer, not guaranteed. Trap? A named r value reference is an l value.

scenes.say: What is a void pointer? An address with no type. How do you use it? Cast back with static cast. Pointer to pointer? One more arrow. Why? To change the caller's pointer, or for argv.
lines: void*: an address with no type.
Use it: cast back with static_cast.
Pointer to pointer: one more arrow, to change the caller's pointer.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Const int star? Const left of the star locks the value. Int star const? Const right of it locks the pointer. Const int star const? Both locked. And a pointer to const does not make the object const.
rows: the object itself can still change

scenes.say: Return a pointer to a local? The frame dies, so it dangles. Instead? By value, a static, or unique_ptr. Dereference null? Undefined, usually a segfault. Prevent it? Check, or use a reference.

Instead: by value, a static, or unique_ptr.

scenes.say: Array versus pointer? Elements versus an address. Array decay? It converts to a pointer to element zero, losing the length. When not? Size of, ampersand, references. Fix? Array or span.

scenes.say: Solve these three next. LeetCode two oh six, reverse linked list, is pointer re-pointing in a loop. LeetCode one forty one, linked list cycle, uses two pointers on a chain. LeetCode nineteen, remove nth node from end, needs a pointer to the link you edit.
